# Bootstrapping an AI-Native Ecosystem {#sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem}

::: {.epigraph}
> "The more designers involved in using the new methods, and the better they are able to communicate with each other, the faster the process of cultural integration runs."
>
> — Lynn Conway, *The MPC Adventures* [@Conway1981MPCAdventures, p. 2]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *What must exist beyond any one team for AI-native architecture claims to become comparable, and how much of it can a single team adopt without waiting?*

**Core thesis:** *Scaling AI-native architecture requires shared community infrastructure (open process data, neutral benchmark governance, and shared verification access), while individual teams can adopt rigorous reporting and matched baselines immediately.*
:::

The preceding chapters examined AI-native design from the perspective of a single engineering organization, yet no individual team can build a scientific discipline on its own. An architecture group can retain failed tool runs, measure its workflow costs, and tighten its baseline comparisons without waiting for a community standard, but better local recordkeeping alone cannot make another organization's parser interpret an exported record correctly, establish a neutral public benchmark, or open access to a semiconductor fabrication line.

That boundary appears the moment a claim leaves the team's own repository (@fig-ch12-cover-map). Once a group asserts that a candidate design transfers cleanly to another toolchain, closes timing at a target process node, or beats competing architectures on a public leaderboard, the claim depends on shared record contracts, qualified process design kits (PDKs) and fabrication paths, or neutral benchmark governance and dispute resolution. The proposals in this chapter connect the limits encountered earlier in the book to shared infrastructure the community could build; their adoption and effectiveness remain to be proved in practice, and none of them gives a team reason to delay its own local engineering discipline.

![**Local engineering practices proceed immediately, while cross-organizational claims require shared infrastructure.** The top tier shows practices an individual team can enforce inside its own repository (lineage tracking, negative-result retention, and matched baselines), whereas the three lower branches trace the external community schemas, fabrication shuttles, and consortium rules required when claims cross organizational boundaries.](images/ch12-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch12-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Overview diagram distinguishing unilateral local engineering practices from shared community infrastructure dependencies. A top panel details immediate local capabilities in lineage tracking, negative-result retention, and baseline matching, while three lower branches detail external requirements for cross-team comparisons, physical or silicon signoff, and public benchmark programs."}

## Why Shared Infrastructure Must Precede Shared Benchmarks {#sec-staging-sequence}

Very-large-scale integration (VLSI) design faced a similar coordination bottleneck in autumn 1979, when Lynn Conway organized the ARPANET-enabled Multi-Project Chip (MPC79) run[^fn-mpc79-mosis-c12] [@MeadConway1980VLSI; @Conway1981MPCAdventures]. Up to that point, custom silicon research had been throttled because circuit layout remained tied to the proprietary fabrication rules of individual foundries. The scalable $\lambda$-based design rules of Mead and Conway separated layout geometry from many process-specific details, while Xerox PARC merged layout files that university designers transmitted over ARPANET into shared mask sets. That shared workflow lowered the cost barrier to physical silicon enough that eighty-two student and research projects could be fabricated on shared Hewlett-Packard wafers and returned as packaged chips within weeks, and it established a multi-project wafer (MPW) model that the MOSIS broker service, funded by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), sustained across four decades of university VLSI exploration [@MOSIS1981VLSI].

[^fn-mpc79-mosis-c12]: **Multi-project chip infrastructure and silicon brokering**: MPC79 aggregated 82 VLSI design projects from 124 designers across roughly a dozen universities over ARPANET email to Xerox PARC, which merged the layouts into 12 die types on two mask sets; Micro-Mask produced the masks and Hewlett-Packard fabricated the wafers [@Conway1981MPCAdventures]. The subsequent DARPA-sponsored MOSIS service formalized this silicon broker model by amortizing fixed photolithographic mask costs across participating academic institutions [@MOSIS1981VLSI].

Computer architecture now faces a comparable access problem across the operational layers of @sec-three-operational-layers. While published Layer 1 and Layer 2 methods such as AlphaChip and AutoTVM already run inside individual organizations using the tools their developers can reach, testing a Layer 3 claim requires following candidate designs across software, microarchitecture, and physical implementation. When an independent group tries to reproduce those checks at a commercial node, it needs access to the corresponding tool licenses, cell libraries, and foundry process decks, while fabricating leading-edge silicon adds mask-set costs estimated in the tens of millions of dollars [@Patel2022MaskSetCosts]. Open data schemas, machine-verifiable tool contracts, reproducible multi-project shuttles, and shared failure repositories are proposed ways to widen that access in the spirit of the Conway precedent, though whether they would change what AI-native design systems can achieve remains to be established, and the ownership boundaries of @sec-what-architect-owns still hold for any shared infrastructure that independent checks require.

Without shared interfaces, deploying closed-loop search risks deepening existing fragmentation in electronic design automation (EDA). A learned placer, for instance, often relies on behaviors specific to one tool version, standard-cell library, or process deck; those assumptions stay hidden as long as the method runs inside its home environment, but surface immediately when another team tries to transfer it. A design system that carries a candidate across tools and organizations therefore needs explicit agreements that make those dependencies visible.

Six proposals address different parts of that coordination problem, with @tbl-ecosystem-staging-sequence pairing each cross-team dependency with the earlier technical limit or risk that motivates it.

| **Proposal** | **Ecosystem action** | **Coordination dependency** | **Earlier limit or risk** |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Shared data schemas and tool contracts | Cross-team comparison needs common semantics for identities, status, units, and tool results. | Tool-specific wrappers and limits on model transfer across tool flows (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces, @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack). |
| 2 | Open implementation paths and cloud silicon shuttles | Silicon claims need a manufacturable process design kit (PDK), an accepted fabrication path, and device measurements; commercial-node signoff needs foundry-qualified decks, libraries, tools, and access. | Physical timing, power-delivery, and thermal checks left unmeasured (@sec-what-architect-owns). |
| 3 | Consortium governance and matched benchmarks | A public leaderboard needs neutral rules, shared task versions, audit capacity, and comparator governance. | Benchmark-health and matched-baseline risks (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect). |
| 4 | Grand challenges and architecture contests | Cross-organization contests depend on stable interfaces, comparable checks, and enforceable resource accounting. | Benchmark gaming, proxy exploitation, and stagnant static comparators (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect). |
| 5 | Public repositories of failed attempts | Shared repositories need schemas, privacy and licensing rules, stewardship, and controls against misleading or unsafe data. | Censored and purged failed runs (@sec-data-representations-world-models). |
| 6 | University curricula and workflow review | A badge needs published criteria, trained reviewers, appeals, maintenance, and evidence that the badge predicts the claimed practice. | Apprenticeship gap and erosion of structural debugging competence under routine automation (@sec-what-architect-owns). |
: **Local adoption can proceed in parallel; shared claims create dependencies.** Each proposal names the infrastructure required before a team makes broader cross-organizational, silicon, or certification claims; the local practices a team can adopt first are collected in @tbl-unilateral-adoption-checklist. This is a dependency map, not a program that has been run. {#tbl-ecosystem-staging-sequence tbl-colwidths="[8,24,36,32]"}

Among the six proposals in @tbl-ecosystem-staging-sequence, four respond directly to technical limits encountered in earlier chapters, whereas grand challenges and workflow badges are proposals for organizing shared research and review rather than remedies tested in the book's worked studies. A contest could focus several groups on one unresolved problem, while a single group can already run a narrow, evaluator-owned challenge that includes a credible baseline and names its untested conditions; similarly, a badge could make the exact scope of a workflow review explicit. Both organizational proposals remain sketches whose practical value would need to be tested.

While multi-stakeholder standards consortia, cloud silicon shuttles, and shared public repositories require collective community investment, an individual research group or industrial team need not wait to adopt the six local practices in @tbl-unilateral-adoption-checklist. Those local practices still consume internal resources: tool logs may already record wall-clock time and accelerator hours, but tracking license checkouts and human triage time can require extra instrumentation, retaining failed runs demands storage and enough context to interpret them later, and running a matched baseline spends evaluation budget. Because a team can plan and control those internal costs directly, whereas agreement on what another organization will accept is a separate external dependency, a student or small laboratory can begin a rigorous local study without claiming that the shared infrastructure already exists.

| **Focus Area** | **Actionable Practice** | **Verification Mechanism** |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **1. Provenance Pinning** | Hash the initial register-transfer level (RTL) files and prompts, and record seeds, tool versions, and compiler flags. | Reject runs that lack lineage headers, and do not report numbers from unversioned working branches. |
| **2. Negative-Result Retention** | Persist unroutable floorplans, timing violations, and solver timeouts in structured execution records. | Prevent silent purging of failed attempts; treat negative runs as essential data for surrogate calibration. |
| **3. Matched Non-Learned Baselines** | Compare learned generators and surrogate optimizers with a strong non-learned baseline (simulated annealing, random search, expert heuristics). | Match compute, license, and human triage budgets across both arms, or report the difference. |
| **4. Sealed Evaluator Boundaries** | Mount timing constraints (SDC), power intent (UPF), and golden testbenches in read-only volumes. | Prevent automated design loops from modifying, weakening, or waiving their own grading criteria. |
| **5. Total-Cost Accounting** | Record the three-tuple $C_{\text{workflow}} = \langle C_{\text{compute}}, C_{\text{license}}, C_{\text{human}} \rangle$. | Measure whether apparent latency gains were bought by burning excessive compute or human engineering hours. |
| **6. Physical Grounding Audits** | Audit fast screening proxies against physical implementation and timing analysis (OpenROAD and OpenSTA with declared PDKs and parasitics) at decision boundaries. | Quantify the stronger-check gap to detect proxy gaming, routing congestion, and unmodeled RC wire delays. |
: **Local practices a single design team can adopt without outside agreement.** Each consumes the team's own storage, evaluation budget, or engineering time, but none depends on another organization accepting it. {#tbl-unilateral-adoption-checklist tbl-colwidths="[22,46,32]"}


When teams do move beyond internal studies to build shared infrastructure, four concurrent workstreams organize the effort (@fig-ecosystem-roadmap): open foundations, consortium governance, community evaluation, and workforce skills. Open foundations connect tool interfaces to accessible implementation paths; governance defines how results are audited and disputed; evaluation exercises those rules through matched benchmark suites and red-teaming contests; and skills curricula prepare practitioners to question generated design collateral. These workstreams develop in parallel rather than in lockstep, because a benchmark suite cannot mandate a physical signoff check that participating academic laboratories lack the tools or process licenses to execute.

![**Ecosystem workstreams share operational dependencies without imposing a rigid sequence.** Four tracks cover open foundations, consortium governance, community evaluation, and workforce skills, linked by dashed connectors where cross-team claims exchange schemas and qualification criteria, with a bottom return path carrying negative design attempts back into the foundations.](images/fig-ecosystem-roadmap){#fig-ecosystem-roadmap width="80%" fig-alt="Roadmap diagram in which four coordinating workstreams cover open foundations, governance, evaluation, and skills and review. Actions span schemas, physical-design paths, matched benchmarks, contests, failure repositories, curricula, and review. Dashed connectors indicate shared dependencies rather than a universal adoption sequence, and a feedback arrow returns negative attempts to the foundations."}

Across those parallel tracks, a closed feedback loop returns negative design attempts directly to the shared foundations. Concrete records of unroutable placements, negative timing slack, and Unified Power Format (UPF) power-domain conflicts expose missing schema fields, unmodeled physical design-rule checks, or omitted benchmark constraints, while supplying observations near physical feasibility boundaries that help calibrate learned surrogates. The horizontal connectors in @fig-ecosystem-roadmap mark the dependencies a team takes on when it asserts a cross-organizational claim; work that stays local needs no prior consortium approval.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Anchor AI-Native Design Systems in Open Foundations"}
**The principle:** Develop shared interfaces, reference paths, and comparison practices around the checks that independent teams need to perform. Open schemas, accessible implementation flows, neutral benchmarks, and qualified failure repositories are proposed ways to make that work possible.

**The application:** Begin local cost, provenance, failure-retention, and comparison practices now. Require shared contracts whenever claims cross team boundaries, support physical claims with a qualified implementation path and silicon claims with retained measurements from fabricated devices, and state the exact scope reviewed for any certification claim.
:::

## Shared Data Schemas and Tool Contracts {#sec-standardized-data-lineage}

Consider what happens when a retained study record reaches another team's tool flow. A reported timing slack value is useful only if the record also states its units, operating corner, and constraint status. When an optimizer exchanges spatial coordinates or power-domain declarations through ad hoc strings, a downstream parser can accept the input while silently assigning it the wrong physical meaning; similarly, if missing measurements are encoded as zeros, a surrogate model can mistake an unmeasured wire delay or resistance for a measured zero and rank a flawed candidate too favorably. The transfer problem of @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack therefore begins before any model makes a prediction: the participating organizations must first agree on what the exchanged state means.

That need for explicit contracts grows as human engineers step out of the handoff loop between tools. When an architect uses a Layer 1 point assistant, that engineer bridges semantic discrepancies between tools by interpreting ambiguous error messages and supplying missing timing corners by hand, whereas a Layer 2 optimizer working inside a single tool container can rely on that tool's internal scripting interface. Once a Layer 3 system coordinates compilers, synthesis, and physical signoff tools without a person checking each boundary, however, it loses that manual repair, and ad hoc wrapper scripts become a source of silent misinterpretation unless explicit, machine-verifiable contracts declare search bounds, execution lineage, and environmental assumptions across organizational boundaries.

Just as the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 1666 (SystemC) standard established common modeling semantics across commercial and open environments [@IEEE2011SystemC1666], a standards consortium (such as MLCommons[^fn-mlcommons-c12] or CHIPS Alliance) could standardize tool and record interfaces before proprietary silos lock in competing application programming interfaces (APIs). Open schema contracts allow generators, surrogate models, and verification engines to interact across organizational boundaries through stable, machine-verifiable specifications. The proposed Open Agentic Interface would formalize this coordination through three complementary record schemas (@fig-oai-schemas):

[^fn-mlcommons-c12]: **Consortium governance in MLCommons and CHIPS Alliance**: Industry consortia such as MLCommons (which maintains MLPerf) and CHIPS Alliance define shared benchmarks, open hardware standards, and multi-stakeholder governance models [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf]. A dedicated Architecture Automation Working Group could adopt practices such as MLPerf's closed and open divisions, submitter review of results, open rules committees, and dispute-resolution procedures to standardize closed-loop exploration benchmarks.

- **Design problem formulations.** Each formulation declares the permitted design changes, locked constraints, evaluation checks, and acceptance criteria ($s_{\text{design}}$), preserving the status and scope of the study. For example, the prospective Lighthouse cache study (@sec-architecture-20-ontology and @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces) sweeps a single parameter (`l2.capacity` at 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB) against fixed cache policies and interfaces, deriving bank count and static random-access memory macro organization from capacity under a declared rule, whereas the executed array study (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization and @sec-feedback-verification-trust) bounds processing-element geometries at 1,024 elements against a mandatory 32 by 32 baseline. Because the Lighthouse extended-reality (XR) challenge supplies a 3\ W thermal design power target for the compute subsystem and an illustrative 120\ frames per second operating point (roughly 8.33\ ms per frame), a formulation must also state which components the power budget covers, which stages share the frame deadline, and how their execution overlaps, details that the array study's simulator returns alone do not establish. Finally, the formulation must identify the technology target, distinguishing a predictive PDK such as ASAP7 from commercial signoff on a node such as TSMC N3E, and describe any changed hardware or software interfaces and obligations so the receiving team can determine which earlier checks still apply.
- **Lineage headers.** These headers record candidate artifacts, parent inputs, transformations, tool flags, structural representations, and environment configurations ($s_{\text{env}}$). While a cryptographic hash identifies exact bytes and an authenticated Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) attestation binds an issuer to a declaration [@SLSA2026Framework],[^fn-slsa-attestation-c12] neither mechanism proves semantic correctness, and an attestation remains only as trustworthy as its builder, signing key, and storage path. Rather than relying on informal logs, lineage headers track the exact inputs and environments used to generate an artifact such as a SystemC memory controller or a high-level synthesis kernel (@sec-data-representations-world-models) by retaining structured records of prompt and commit hashes, intermediate representations such as abstract syntax trees, control-data flow graphs, and Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) or Circuit Intermediate Representation Compilers and Tools (CIRCT) dialects, execution seeds, and environment definitions (container digests and command-line interface (CLI) arguments). A team might therefore export structural hashes, compiler pass fingerprints, and bounding-box geometry metrics while withholding internal transistor topologies, unreleased instruction-set-architecture opcodes, and proprietary foundry cell libraries, although those summaries still require disclosure review to assess what several records reveal together.
- **Multi-fidelity environmental contracts and programmatic tool qualification.** Environmental contracts specify typed input prerequisites, output schemas, declared error assumptions, status semantics, and property-appropriate checks across analytical models, cycle-level simulators, and register-transfer level (RTL) tools. Qualification checks verify whether tools such as gem5, Verilator, SCALE-Sim, Ramulator, OpenROAD, Yosys, and OpenSTA expose pinned container interfaces, structured state exports, checkpoint behavior, machine-parsable failures, and documented checks (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces). For formal tools, the contract must also record proof scope: SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) state properties that bounded model checking (BMC) can check within a declared execution bound and under stated assumptions.[^fn-bmc-c12] A passing bounded check therefore needs a separate completeness argument to establish the property for all executions of the model, and still cannot exclude a deadlock or other behavior the model omits.

[^fn-slsa-attestation-c12]: **Software supply chain attestations and SLSA**: The SLSA framework provides machine-readable specifications for artifact build provenance. While SLSA Build Level 1 provenance can remain unsigned, higher levels require cryptographically authenticated provenance [@SLSA2026Framework]. A cryptographic signature authenticates the issuer's declaration about the builder and execution environment; its evidentiary value depends on trust in that issuer, and it does not verify semantic circuit correctness.

[^fn-bmc-c12]: **Bounded model checking and completeness thresholds**: Bounded model checking searches circuit executions up to a finite depth ($k$ cycles) for counterexamples to an encoded property [@BiereEtAl1999BMC]. Passing that bound alone does not establish unbounded correctness. For a finite-state model, a sufficiently large bound can establish the property if a completeness threshold or recurrence diameter for that specific model and property has been formally justified.

![**Open Agentic Interface schemas decouple tool orchestration from proprietary data formats.** Design problem formulations declare search bounds and system obligations; lineage headers bind artifacts to cryptographically signed transformations; and environmental contracts specify tool prerequisites, assumptions, and checks. Together they are intended to allow selective cross-organizational exchange without exposing proprietary transistor netlists. The schema is proposed, and the fields shown are illustrative examples drawn from the book's two studies.](images/fig-oai-schemas){#fig-oai-schemas width="80%" fig-alt="Diagram of three proposed Open Agentic Interface record schemas, showing design problem formulations, lineage headers, and environmental contracts feeding sequentially into a selective metadata exchange governed by independent trust and access policies."}

In implementing the three schemas of @fig-oai-schemas, serialization syntax remains a transport choice rather than the semantic contract itself. Protocol Buffers provide typed message schemas and high-throughput binary serialization, whereas JSON-LD connects execution records to shared vocabularies through persistent web identifiers, yet neither format alone resolves the physical meaning of a tool output. When a receiving tool uses a lineage header to locate an implementation artifact (such as a static timing report) and confirm that its contents match the declared cryptographic hash, the parser must still inspect the enclosing environmental contract to verify schema versions, operating corners, slack units, and execution status, and must never let missing values default to zero slack. Working together, the formulation defines the search boundary, the lineage header authenticates the artifact, and the environmental contract supplies the interpretation rules, which can support selective cross-organizational exchange while proprietary cell libraries and unreleased microarchitectural topologies stay inside each organization.

Rather than replacing the structural formats that hardware flows already use, the Open Agentic Interface would record how tools and generators act on them. Where CIRCT and MLIR standardize the structural syntax of hardware modules and compiler dialects, and established interchange formats such as LEF/DEF for physical geometry, IEEE 1801 UPF for power intent, OpenAccess[^fn-openaccess-c12] for design databases, and FIRRTL for generator output represent the design itself, the workflow schemas carry the surrounding record of how a run manipulated those artifacts. Because those records serve different roles over time, each schema class has its own durability requirement: problem formulations must retain their exact meaning after external parsing, lineage headers must remain interpretable apart from the original execution container, and environmental contracts must make changes in tool behavior explicit whenever a simulator or synthesis tool is updated.

[^fn-openaccess-c12]: **OpenAccess design database standard**: OpenAccess is an industry-standard binary database and API managed by the Silicon Integration Initiative for representing integrated circuit design objects, hierarchy, and physical connectivity across EDA tools. High-level workflow schemas complement OpenAccess by standardizing orchestration, attempt lineage, and property assertions across tools rather than managing in-memory physical geometries.

Even a well-specified schema gains traction only if design teams require compatible exports from the tools they procure and contribute conformance tests that check how those exports are interpreted. Shared customer demand could reduce repeated wrapper maintenance and let teams compare tool behavior on identical inputs, provided the consortium maintains compatibility tests as tools and schemas evolve. Agreeing on how to exchange timing and layout records addresses only half of the cross-team validation problem, however; independent researchers also need legal and technical access to the physical implementation flows that produce those records.

## Precompetitive Open Infrastructure and Shared Tooling {#sec-precompetitive-infrastructure}

In deep-submicron and nanoscale fabrication, evaluating routing congestion, power-grid IR drop,[^fn-ir-drop-c12] UPF power-domain isolation, thermal dissipation, and manufacturability requires implementation evidence calibrated to the target node. Because device structures, manufacturing rules, and interconnect resistance and capacitance[^fn-rc-parasitics-c12] vary sharply with the process and interact with the placed and routed layout, a nominal node label alone cannot establish that a candidate architecture will close timing. Commercial foundries protect those process details behind strict nondisclosure agreements (NDAs), proprietary signoff tools, and restricted design-rule manuals, which leaves academic laboratories and early-stage startups with a structural barrier to physical design exploration.[^fn-pdk-lockin-c12]

[^fn-ir-drop-c12]: **Static and dynamic voltage droop**: Voltage degradation across the power distribution network arises from static resistive loss ($V = I \times R$) through metal grids and dynamic inductive droop ($V = L \cdot di/dt$) during simultaneous clock-edge switching surges. Localized dynamic droop degrades gate switching speeds and introduces transient timing violations that nominal static timing analysis fails to capture.

[^fn-rc-parasitics-c12]: **Nanoscale interconnect parasitics**: At advanced semiconductor nodes (7\ nm and below), wire cross-sections shrink, and surface and grain-boundary scattering together with the resistive barrier layer raise effective copper resistivity sharply. For long wires, delay through on-chip wire resistance ($R$) and parasitic capacitance ($C$) can exceed gate delay, requiring macro placers and routers to optimize for layer-dependent wire characteristics rather than planar wirelength alone.

[^fn-pdk-lockin-c12]: **Proprietary isolation in physical design kits**: Foundry access agreements and disclosure restrictions limit which researchers can rerun an implementation study or inspect its design-rule assumptions. Review by another authorized industrial team may still be possible, but it remains distinct from open scientific reproduction.

Open-source physical-design infrastructure and MPW shuttle access narrow this divide for public research. Whereas a Layer 2 study that stays within one organization's licensed tools and closed commercial PDKs can be checked internally even if outsiders cannot rerun it, a Layer 3 system relies on physical checks to decide which candidates advance, so a claim about such a system can be reproduced openly only where independent teams can run those same checks. Open PDKs, including SkyWater SKY130 (130\ nm CMOS) [@SkyWater2020SKY130PDK], IHP SG13G2 (130\ nm BiCMOS), and GlobalFoundries GF180MCU (180\ nm), expose device models, standard cells, and design rules for research on manufacturable processes, although targeting a manufacturable line does not make every open PDK release production-qualified and fabrication still requires a kit release and rule checks accepted by the chosen service [@IHPOpenPDK; @GlobalFoundriesGF180MCUOpenPDK]. Coupled with the CIRCT and MLIR compiler infrastructure [@CIRCT] and open EDA engines (OpenROAD, Yosys, and OpenSTA), these open PDKs let researchers inspect and version more of the implementation flow at mature nodes. Reproducing a result still requires retaining the inputs, tool versions, constraints, and execution records, and a mature-node open flow never stands in for signoff at an advanced commercial node.

When a design team builds on established synthesis, layout, and simulation infrastructure, it can concentrate effort on candidate microarchitectures and constraint formulations rather than re-implementing baseline toolchains. Tool and library reuse does not confer inherited correctness, however: a generated macro still requires full signoff checks in its concrete integration context, even when its upstream toolchain and neighboring IP blocks have been exercised in prior tapeouts. Shared open-source dependencies make verification environments easier for other groups to reproduce, but they never render new architectural compositions pre-verified.

When a study needs to model deep-nanoscale scaling trends without commercial foundry access, academic groups often rely on ASAP7, a predictive 7\ nm PDK built for scaling projections rather than manufacturable signoff [@ClarkEtAl2016ASAP7].[^fn-predictive-pdk-c12] Because its device models, design rules, and extraction decks do not target a physical foundry line, a candidate architecture that ranks well on ASAP7 power, performance, and area (PPA) may still fail timing closure or routing congestion constraints under commercial foundry design rules, and its estimates cannot substitute for signoff against a commercial process's qualified decks. Any claim that predictive-PDK evaluations track commercial TSMC N7, N3, or N2 characteristics therefore requires a separate validation study with matched industrial baselines, documented modeling assumptions, and an explicit assessment of where predicted and reference results diverge.

[^fn-predictive-pdk-c12]: **Predictive process design kits**: A predictive PDK is a collection of device models and design rules developed to model projected physical scaling trends rather than support manufacturing on a qualified commercial line. The 7\ nm ASAP7 library provides an openly accessible academic example [@ClarkEtAl2016ASAP7].

## Silicon Shuttles and Cost Reduction {#sec-silicon-shuttles}

Pre-silicon tools can estimate timing, power delivery, and thermal behavior before fabrication, yet every pre-silicon check is bounded by the accuracy of its device models, extracted parasitics, operating conditions, and package assumptions: whereas a predictive kit supports comparisons only within that modeled environment and foundry-qualified analysis supports a pre-silicon implementation claim, empirical validation requires measurements on a fabricated die. Closing the unmeasured physical checks in @sec-what-architect-owns therefore calls for a named implementation or measurement path rather than an undifferentiated demand for silicon. MPW shuttles address that final step by splitting fixed mask and wafer costs across many research designs in the MPC79 and MOSIS precedent [@Conway1981MPCAdventures; @MOSIS1981VLSI]; because each participant pays only a small fraction of the fixed tooling cost, open educational shuttles now draw thousands of design submissions at mature nodes (@fig-ch12-money-plot-tapeout-cost-collapse).

![**Open mature-node shuttles have drawn thousands of design submissions.** Designs submitted per Tiny Tapeout run on SkyWater SKY130, IHP SG13G2, and GlobalFoundries GF180MCU (bars, hatched by process), with the cumulative total reaching 4,026 across 22 runs in an August 2026 catalog snapshot (line) [@TinyTapeoutRunCatalog]. Counts include test shuttles and runs not yet delivered; they measure participation, not fabricated or working silicon, and say nothing about advanced-node signoff.](images/fig-shuttle-cost-democratization){#fig-ch12-money-plot-tapeout-cost-collapse width="80%" fig-alt="Bar chart with a cumulative line of design submissions per Tiny Tapeout shuttle run from 2022 to 2026. Bars for 22 runs range from about 30 to 547 designs, distinguished by fill pattern for the SkyWater, IHP, and GlobalFoundries processes, and the cumulative line rises from 152 to 4,026 designs."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
import json as _json12tt
from pathlib import Path as _Path12tt
import _python.plots as _ap12tt

_tt17 = _json12tt.loads(
    (_Path12tt(_ap12tt.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
     / "data" / "studies" / "17-silicon-report-coverage" / "summary.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
)
tt17_macros = _tt17["population_macro_rows"]
tt17_with_fb = _tt17["macros_with_any_public_feedback"]
tt17_with_pct = f"{_tt17['macro_feedback_presence_percent']:.1f}"
tt17_no_fb = _tt17["macros_without_public_feedback"]
tt17_no_pct = f"{100 - _tt17['macro_feedback_presence_percent']:.1f}"
tt17_records = _tt17["community_feedback_records"]
```

Shared wafer runs provide access to a qualitatively different experimental regime rather than a discounted equivalent of commercial fabrication. Full-reticle mask tooling at leading-edge nodes is estimated in the tens of millions of dollars [@Patel2022MaskSetCosts], a barrier few research groups can cross without industrial backing.[^fn-mask-costs-c12] Multiplexed open-process tiles, by contrast, lower the entry cost for a small digital design to a few hundred dollars [@TinyTapeout2025TTSky25aSubmitted],[^fn-tinytapeout-architecture-c12] so teams can run physical bring-up, digital functional verification, and basic telemetry at clock rates in the tens of megahertz. While measurements on mature planar nodes (such as 130\ nm and 180\ nm) cannot establish sub-5\ nm closure, where device structures, routing geometries, power densities, clock networks, and packaging conditions differ markedly, bench testing can still expose real timing failures, voltage droop, and packaging effects within the chosen vehicle and close the diagnostic loop between simulation and measured silicon inside a declared operating envelope.

Even so, the submission growth in @fig-ch12-money-plot-tapeout-cost-collapse reflects broad community participation rather than verified silicon yield: several of the plotted runs had not yet delivered chips at the time of the snapshot, and even on delivered runs public bring-up reporting remains voluntary and sparse. Across all `{python} tt17_macros` macros on the delivered Tiny Tapeout 06 (`TT06`) shuttle [@TinyTapeout2026TT06Feedback], `{python} tt17_with_fb` macros (`{python} tt17_with_pct`%) have any public community feedback entry (`{python} tt17_records` feedback records in total), while `{python} tt17_no_fb` macros (`{python} tt17_no_pct`%) have no public silicon report; that gap marks an absence of public bring-up evidence rather than a verified silicon failure. An architectural claim on a shared shuttle therefore reaches only as far as the retained bench measurements, operating envelope, die area, pad interfaces, and instrumentation that the chosen vehicle provides.

[^fn-mask-costs-c12]: **Photolithographic mask tooling and respin economics**: Advanced process nodes that use extreme ultraviolet lithography require dozens of reticles, and optical proximity correction and multi-patterning push mask-set costs up steeply. One analyst estimate places a mask set above \$1 million at 28\ nm, above \$10 million at 7\ nm, and near \$40 million approaching 3\ nm [@Patel2022MaskSetCosts]; published estimates vary widely by node, foundry, and layer count. If an escaped defect cannot be adequately contained through firmware or validated operating restrictions, correcting it may require revised masks and another fabrication run (a silicon respin). That revision can add months of foundry delay and further non-recurring engineering costs.

[^fn-tinytapeout-architecture-c12]: **Multiplexed open-shuttle tiles**: Educational shuttles achieve substantial cost reductions by tiling hundreds of independent digital designs onto a single shared silicon die. A centralized digital multiplexer connects the shared clock, reset, and a small set of input, output, and bidirectional pins to one selected design at a time, restricting digital submissions to modest frequencies (tens of megahertz), small standard-cell counts, and low-speed interfaces without dedicated high-speed pads. Some shuttles also offer analog tiles with a few dedicated pins.

Existing shuttle programs illustrate both the variety of shared fabrication paths and their dependence on institutional continuity. Tiny Tapeout's public run catalog and Europractice's MPW service provide different routes to shared fabrication [@TinyTapeoutRunCatalog; @EuropracticeMPWPrototyping]. At the same time, Google's 2022 announcement of Google-funded GF180MCU Open MPW runs with Efabless [@Google2022OpenMPW], followed by Efabless's closure in early 2025 [@TinyTapeout2025EfablessShutsDown] and Tiny Tapeout's shift to a different service for SkyWater runs [@TinyTapeout2025TTSky25aSubmitted], shows that shared fabrication access depends on the survival of the organizations that broker it. Because these programs differ in submission interfaces, process access, and implementation requirements, a team must check the active terms and accepted PDK release for its planned run. When teams use such shuttles to evaluate automatically generated macros, the test vehicle also needs shared on-chip characterization infrastructure. A research shuttle can allocate isolated power-monitored rails, ring oscillators, and on-chip transient voltage droop monitors for timing and power-delivery characterization across voltage and temperature,[^fn-ring-oscillators-c12] alongside JTAG interfaces for collecting telemetry, but those features have to be designed into the vehicle and qualified rather than assumed from booking space on a shared wafer.

[^fn-ring-oscillators-c12]: **On-chip ring oscillators and droop monitors for silicon characterization**: A ring oscillator is an on-chip test structure consisting of an odd number of inverting logic gates in a closed feedback loop whose natural oscillation frequency directly reflects stage gate delay. Fabricating arrays of ring oscillators and localized high-bandwidth voltage droop detectors across varying cell types, metal layers, and supply rails allows characterization teams to measure true local gate delay, dynamic $IR$-drop transients, and intra-die process variation across voltage and temperature, providing ground-truth measurements to calibrate multi-fidelity timing and power models.

With qualified characterization structures in place, a retained measurement campaign can connect each fabricated candidate to its bench timing and power observations and to the pre-silicon models that predicted them. That link gives the community a path to calibrating surrogates against measured silicon rather than only against another EDA tool, even though any yield claim still requires an appropriate population of devices and test conditions. Containerized open flows improve repeatability for the pre-silicon half of those campaigns, though they neither grant commercial-tool rights nor close the physical gap to a different foundry process.[^fn-eda-eula-restrictions-c12]

[^fn-eda-eula-restrictions-c12]: **Commercial EDA licensing restrictions and closed data models**: A study using commercial EDA tools must establish what its licenses permit, including automated execution, access by another team, and publication of comparative runtime or PPA results. These permissions must be checked for the applicable agreement. Proprietary databases and closed timing-graph representations can also restrict programmatic access, pushing automated workflows toward brittle tool-control wrappers that complicate reproducible interaction and headless cloud orchestration.

## Consortium Governance and Benchmarking {#sec-neutral-governance}

Shared schemas, open implementation flows, and silicon shuttles let an individual team produce auditable physical evidence, but comparing results across teams still requires agreement on the experiment itself. If groups evaluate different RTL blocks, leave compute hours uncounted, or tune prompts on the test tasks, a reported margin can mix genuine architectural improvement with unequal search budgets and selection effects, including the optimizer's curse (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization). Shared tasks, reference baselines, disclosure rules, and audit procedures are needed to counter these benchmark-health risks (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect).

Drawing on the governance model of MLCommons[^fn-mlcommons-c12] and MLPerf [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf], an independent Architecture Automation Working Group hosted by an established body (such as MLCommons,[^fn-mlcommons-c12] the Standard Performance Evaluation Corporation, CHIPS Alliance, or the IEEE Council on Electronic Design Automation) could maintain those shared rules and adjudicate disputed results. While isolating the contribution of any single method still requires the controlled ablations of @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect, a consortium working group could organize cross-team comparisons around three core responsibilities:

- **Reference problem suites.** The consortium would maintain problem suites grounded in realistic industrial constraints, spanning 3\ W mobile XR spatial processing, RISC-V RV64GCV vector clusters, datacenter tensor acceleration, Compute Express Link memory expansion, and Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express chiplet interconnect management. Although open automated flows can explore and synthesize digital controller logic, packet arbiters, and link-layer state machines, physical-layer analog front-ends (including high-speed serializer/deserializer circuits, phase-locked loops, and calibrated impedance terminators) remain proprietary, foundry-specific macros that require dedicated mixed-signal signoff. Each suite would also need active maintainers for its reference implementations and tool configurations, versioned releases, and clear rules for when a bug fix requires prior submissions to be rerun, so that reported gains never rest on a weak or outdated baseline.
- **Closed and open benchmark divisions.** Separate divisions would let researchers answer different comparative questions while keeping resource budgets explicit. A Closed Division would require entrants to compete under locked tool wrappers, fixed compute budgets, and matched baselines so that reviewers can compare search methods on equal footing. An Open Division would allow custom search procedures, domain heuristics, or proprietary surrogates while holding the architectural target fixed and requiring full disclosure of workflow costs and artifact lineage, so that reviewers can compare complete end-to-end approaches under declared conditions.
- **Total workflow-cost accounting.** Every submission would report the full resource vector ($C_{\text{workflow}} = \langle C_{\text{compute}}, C_{\text{license}}, C_{\text{human}} \rangle$) by recording GPU compute hours, EDA license checkout minutes, and human engineering and triage time alongside design quality.

These three responsibilities give research groups a common basis for comparison, but credible governance also depends on how contested results are handled and how scores are interpreted. Before accepting submissions, the working group would need to specify what evidence a formal challenge must supply, how reviewers with conflicts of interest are recused, and when a disputed run must be reproduced, corrected, or withdrawn, and publish its rulings so that similar disputes receive consistent treatment. Every benchmark release should likewise state which physical and system constraints its score captures and which remain untested, so that readers do not treat a gain on a benchmark metric as proof of transfer to production designs.[^fn-contest-benchmarks-c12]

[^fn-contest-benchmarks-c12]: **Overfitting in competitive benchmarks**: An optimization method can improve scores on a fixed benchmark suite without generalizing to real-world industrial circuit designs. Evaluators must distinguish performance gains on the declared challenge from verified transfer to production workloads.

## Grand Challenges and Design Contests {#sec-grand-challenges}

Static benchmark suites alone rarely force a field to confront its hardest failure modes: left to individual paper submissions, research groups naturally gravitate toward isolated subproblems where their methods already perform well, while cross-layer bottlenecks such as closing physical timing under strict power limits or catching subtle verification loopholes go untested under head-to-head conditions. Once a consortium establishes neutral baseline rules and cost accounting, recurring design contests can use that infrastructure to focus the community on those neglected bottlenecks. Computer architecture already relies on shared traces and evaluation rules in the Championship Branch Prediction [@CBP2016BranchPrediction] and Data Prefetching Championship [@DPC2015DataPrefetching] series, often built on the ChampSim simulator [@GoberEtAl2022ChampSim], much as the DARPA Grand Challenges in autonomous vehicles [@BuehlerEtAl2009DARPA; @ThrunEtAl2006Stanley] and ImageNet in computer vision [@RussakovskyEtAl2015ImageNet] rallied their fields around shared tasks. The EDA community has an equally strong contest tradition, including placement in 2005 and global routing in 2007 and 2008 in [ISPD's contest archive](https://www.ispd.cc/contests/08/) and the [CAD Contest at ICCAD](https://www.iccad-contest.org/) launched in 2012. Rather than creating a separate institution, an Architecture 2.0 challenge could run as a track alongside these established venues across three representative problem areas:

- **Constrained physical PPA generation.** Entrants translate a high-level specification into RTL and carry it through a named implementation flow under a fixed power and thermal budget. Submissions are judged on the declared physical checks and human-intervention budget, with the explicit understanding that passing a contest flow does not authorize commercial tapeout.
- **Sample-efficient design-space exploration.** Teams search microarchitectural configurations across heterogeneous workloads under a strict simulation budget and return the nondominated designs found during the run (those that no other evaluated candidate matches on every objective and beats on at least one). One practical scoring rule measures the fraction of pre-declared target bounds reached within the budget, such as meeting both an energy ceiling and a latency bound while passing all feasibility checks; reaching those targets tests sample efficiency under fixed goals without claiming that the true global Pareto frontier has been found.
- **Adversarial red-teaming and hardware security.** Teams audit generated hardware collateral to detect seeded timing exceptions, malicious logic, and verification loopholes. Catching bad timing exceptions requires constraint audits paired with static timing analysis, while SVA and BMC can expose functional violations within a declared model and cycle bound. Scoring would tally the seeded defects caught against false alarms and record which checks found them, which measures coverage of the challenge set rather than proving the absence of every possible Trojan or timing flaw.

Even after a winning contest score is surpassed, the unsuccessful submissions retain scientific value: their inputs and diagnostic logs record which candidate designs broke under the contest's constraints and supply the raw material for a shared repository of failed runs.

## Public Repositories of Failed Runs {#sec-open-failed-attempts}

When a design team treats a failed synthesis or place-and-route run as a wasted experiment and deletes the log, it strips learned surrogates of the observations that map physical limits (@sec-data-representations-world-models). An unroutable floorplan or a negative timing slack report marks a feasibility boundary that a corpus of clean designs never shows, so training only on the survivors leaves those boundaries poorly constrained.[^fn-survivorship-bias-c12] Retaining negative runs gives later studies data near the cliff edge, provided contributors separate genuine design failures from tool crashes or bad settings and remember that a failed run records what happened under specific constraints, tool versions, and budgets rather than proving the architecture itself impossible. A consortium repository needs three elements to make these failed runs reusable across teams:

[^fn-survivorship-bias-c12]: **Survivorship bias in surrogate training data**: Training predictive surrogate models solely on successful, design-rule-clean, and timing-closed implementations creates a truncated sample that omits observed failures. Without examples of unroutable floorplans and severe timing violations, that dataset may poorly constrain the feasibility boundaries a surrogate must predict.

- **Execution traces and run context.** Each entry should preserve CLI logs, tool return codes, standard-error streams, and resource telemetry for failed synthesis, simulation, and place-and-route jobs, along with the inputs, constraints, tool and PDK versions, dependencies, random seeds, and execution budgets. Runs that rely on proprietary or unavailable dependencies can still help diagnose failure modes, provided the record states clearly which steps another laboratory cannot replay.
- **Qualified failure annotations.** A shared taxonomy must separate design-level observations, such as timing violations (worst negative slack $\text{WNS} < 0$),[^fn-wns-tns-c12] design-rule-checking geometry errors, assertion counterexamples, deadlocks, and routing congestion maps, from infrastructure failures such as license timeouts or disk exhaustion. Because a license timeout says nothing about the candidate's feasibility whereas a timing violation characterizes that implementation under its recorded constraints, each annotation should also distinguish the raw symptom observed by the tool from the suspected or confirmed root cause and cite the diagnostic evidence behind that judgment.
- **Disclosure review and filtering.** Sanitization pipelines could convert proprietary physical netlists into normalized graph embeddings, anonymized congestion heatmaps, and relative slack distributions that strip absolute die coordinates, foundry cell-type names, and top-level block pinouts. Because patterns across a series of failed runs can still leak commercial product details that no single record reveals, these transformations require human disclosure review before release, and each published record should state what diagnostic detail was stripped so downstream users know which conclusions the data can still support.

[^fn-wns-tns-c12]: **Worst negative slack and total negative slack**: In static timing analysis, worst negative slack (WNS) measures the timing delay violation on the single most critical endpoint in the design, determining whether the clock frequency target is met. Total negative slack (TNS) sums the negative slack across all violating endpoints; a design with small WNS but large TNS has many failing endpoints, which often points to a systemic cause such as congestion, clock skew, or an unrealistic constraint rather than one isolated path.

OpenROAD-flow-scripts already publishes test results, logs, and artifacts for reproducing failures through its [continuous integration infrastructure](https://openroad-flow-scripts.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contrib/CI.html); a community repository would extend that practice across projects and tool flows by adding shared failure annotations and disclosure review. Such a corpus helps other teams avoid known dead ends and gives multi-fidelity surrogates training points right along the physical feasibility boundary, though keeping those records usable over time requires active maintainers to pin tool dependencies, review annotations, and check whether older runs remain interpretable.[^fn-abandonware-c12] Any team can start internally by saving full run context and separating observed tool symptoms from root-cause diagnoses, while leaving shared taxonomy governance and cross-run disclosure review (@sec-ecosystem-open-questions) to consortium coordination.

[^fn-abandonware-c12]: **Software degradation and infrastructure rot**: Rapid drift in upstream open-source EDA dependencies, Linux kernel libraries, container base images, and external web APIs can render published hardware design flows unreproducible within months. Long-term workflow preservation requires hermetic container digests, pinned tool binaries, and dedicated active stewardship rather than static code archives.

## Sustaining Research and Industrial Adoption {#sec-ecosystem-outlook}

Sustaining these shared workflows in production also requires adapting how commercial EDA tools are licensed. Traditional EDA licensing grew up around engineers at interactive workstations and predictable overnight regressions, a usage profile that point assistance and small Layer 2 sweeps largely preserve. By contrast, a closed-loop exploration harness that launches hundreds of parallel headless tool jobs during a search burst and then sits idle during analysis strains fixed seat allocations. Metered cloud licensing for burst workloads already exists: Synopsys, for example, sells by-the-minute pay-per-use access to its cloud tools under its FlexEDA model [@Synopsys2022FlexEDA; @Synopsys2026Cloud].[^fn-eda-licensing-c12] The open questions are how those pricing models behave at the scale and burstiness of automated exploration, and whether commercial end-user agreements permit the headless execution and public benchmark reporting that cross-organization comparisons require. If shared schemas, open reference flows, and elastic licensing make closed-loop exploration economical, engineering effort could shift further toward problem formulation, cross-layer trade-offs, and signoff review, while lower front-end design costs could make small-volume application-specific integrated circuits viable for academic laboratories and startups whose budgets can still cover masks, packaging, and physical validation. Whether those possibilities materialize, however, depends on more than tool access and licensing: engineers must still develop the diagnostic judgment to audit what automated flows return.

[^fn-eda-licensing-c12]: **EDA burst licensing and commercial friction**: Commercial EDA tools have traditionally been sold as annual term licenses or floating network tokens priced for human design teams. Automated closed-loop exploration generates burst demand, with many parallel tool instances for brief optimization sweeps followed by idle evaluation intervals. Pay-per-use cloud licensing addresses the metering, while vendor end-user agreements, site-locked license daemons, and container startup latency can still limit elastic automated scaling.

## Training Architects for AI-Native Design {#sec-curriculum-certification}

That diagnostic judgment begins in how architects are trained, and the shared records, open implementation flows, and failure repositories described above change what students can practice in the classroom. While writing RTL modules by hand and running individual EDA tools remain essential ways to learn how hardware behaves, students must also learn to formulate architectural hypotheses, choose useful experiments, and determine which parts of that work a learned model can perform. A proposed accelerator gives them two related subjects to investigate: how its organization affects application performance, and how the information and choices available to a model affect the designs it proposes.

An AI-native curriculum should therefore extend quantitative architectural reasoning to the design process itself. Students should predict bottlenecks, construct alternatives, and explain measured outcomes while investigating how workload examples, design representations, tool feedback, and search budgets influence automated exploration. Those investigations require comparisons with analytical models and conventional search methods, with the contribution of each learned component left open to measurement. The six stages of the design loop (@sec-architecture-20-ontology) organize this work around recurring engineering decisions (@tbl-classical-to-ai-native-skills); each laboratory can revisit the complete loop as students gain responsibility for both the proposed system and the experiments used to improve it.

| **Life-cycle stage** | **Foundational skill** | **Conventional practice** | **Role in an automated design loop** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Formulate** | Workload characterization and quantitative reasoning | Profile a benchmark suite to report instruction mix, working-set size, reuse distance, and sparsity for a static report. | Reason across workload byte traffic, numerical precision, and pin bandwidth to decide whether a target fits within Layer 2 tuning or requires Layer 3 co-design, then freeze the evaluation contract and baseline so a search process cannot relax its own constraints. |
| **2. Explore** | Performance bounds | Solve Iron Law, Roofline, Amdahl's Law, and Little's Law equations by hand to explain bottlenecks in an existing design. | Encode conservation-of-bytes floors and queue-sizing bounds as fast pre-simulation filters that reject infeasible candidates in milliseconds, and expose bottleneck and data-reuse telemetry so search converges in far fewer simulator calls. |
| **3. Implement** | Computer arithmetic and microarchitectural organization | Draft a fixed-point datapath or multi-stage pipeline by hand in RTL and debug hazards on directed waveform traces. | Co-design block-quantized number formats, software schedules, and accumulator widths in a bit-exact software reference model that checks generated RTL at module boundaries before full-chip simulation or synthesis runs. |
| **4. Evaluate** | Multi-fidelity simulation, verification, and physical implementation | Run cycle simulation and end-of-project logic synthesis and place-and-route to check whether a hand-written block closes timing and area. | Pair syntax and structural audits with randomized-reset and memory-latency stress tests alongside in-loop synthesis and layout checks to catch simulation-only shortcuts, multiplexer fanout explosions, and unbuffered wire delays that cycle simulation misses. |
| **5. Interpret** | Experimental attribution, root-cause diagnosis, and cost accounting | Compare a small number of manual design points in a lab report and attribute speedup to a single human-selected change. | Require controlled ablations that verify why a candidate improved, route failures back to implementation, exploration, or formulation according to their physical cause, and charge total simulation, tool, and energy cost to the verified outcome. |
| **6. Commit** | Benchmarking methodology, physical signoff, and governance | Submit a final project report summarizing achieved clock frequency, area, and speedup over a starter baseline. | Audit the baseline comparator against strawman inflation, state where pre-layout wireload models or blackboxed memory macros stop short of foundry signoff, verify replay artifacts, and take human accountability for the final commitment decision. |
: **The design loop reorganizes foundational architecture skills around specification, pruning, diagnosis, and signoff.** Each row pairs one stage of the design life cycle (@sec-architecture-20-ontology) with the classical analytical foundation it relies on, its traditional classroom exercise, and the engineering role it serves when an automated loop proposes and evaluates candidate designs. {#tbl-classical-to-ai-native-skills tbl-colwidths="[16,22,26,36]"}

Across the six rows of @tbl-classical-to-ai-native-skills, principles that students once applied by hand to a single design become executable contracts and diagnostic checks at specific stops of the loop. At the formulation stage, textbook recall is not enough [@PrakashEtAl2025QuArch]: before any search begins, the architect must combine workload byte-traffic estimates with pin-bandwidth and area limits to determine whether a target is even reachable inside a frozen hardware template (Layer 2) or requires joint numerical and microarchitectural co-design (Layer 3), while locking the evaluation script so an automated loop cannot pass by lowering its clock target or accuracy threshold. During exploration and implementation, the Roofline model, Amdahl's Law, Little's Law, and computer arithmetic move from post-hoc paper exercises to active loop controls. Conservation-of-bytes floors reject infeasible memory-traffic proposals in milliseconds, structured bottleneck telemetry allows an agentic search to match classical design-space exploration in a fraction of the simulator calls [@WangEtAl2026AgentDSE], and a bit-exact fixed-point reference model separates numerical quantization drift from RTL pipeline stalls before synthesis runs. During evaluation, interpretation, and commitment, physical synthesis and benchmarking rigor move inside the loop because models asked to predict hardware performance without simulator feedback routinely misjudge outcomes [@WangEtAl2026ArchEval]: only multi-tier checks, controlled ablations, causal routing back to the stage that failed, and full accounting of simulator calls and energy per verified outcome [@TschandEtAl2024MLPerfPower] give a human reviewer enough evidence to sign off.

Because an automated workflow depends on the architect to write these executable bounds, reference models, and physical checks, delegating first-pass drafting and parameter tuning without replacing the underlying diagnostic practice creates the apprenticeship gap examined in @sec-what-architect-owns. Unless the curriculum rebuilds hands-on contact with timing reports, waveform anomalies, and routing congestion maps, organizations risk holding human architects accountable for signoff decisions they lack the experience to judge (@sec-sustaining-responsibility) [@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones], the skill-erosion trap that Bainbridge identified in automated systems [@Bainbridge1983Ironies].

::: {.callout-law title="Bainbridge's Ironies of Automation in Hardware Design"}
**The Classical Principle:** Automating routine tasks can reduce opportunities to maintain the skills needed when the operator must take over. The remaining faults may demand more experience precisely when routine practice has diminished [@Bainbridge1983Ironies].

**Hardware Design Application:** A summary score can report that a candidate failed without teaching the reviewer how to distinguish a layout problem from an incorrect timing constraint. Training must include the underlying artifacts and the checks that separate those causes.

**Mitigation Strategy:** Implement shadow verification audits and diagnostic fault-injection training to restore the operator's exposure to structural debugging without reverting to routine manual drafting (@sec-law-ironies-automation in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

Two laboratory practices can rebuild that diagnostic experience in a setting where mistakes are safe to investigate before fabrication. In a shadow verification audit, a student follows an automated exploration run, forms an independent hypothesis about the bottleneck the optimizer is targeting, and audits the generated RTL alongside its Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) declarations before comparing that diagnosis against the instructor's review. The student learns by explaining why a reported speedup survives or fails downstream checks rather than merely watching the run finish.

In a companion fault-injection laboratory, instructors seed a candidate design with a clock-domain crossing (CDC) synchronization bug,[^fn-cdc-metastability-c12] an unhandled finite-state-machine reset state, or a silent false path in its SDC file.[^fn-sdc-false-path-c12] Students must choose the right diagnostic check for each fault: structural CDC analysis for unsafe crossings, simulation or formal property checking for reset behavior, and constraint audits for the false path. Because zero-delay RTL simulation cannot observe analog metastability and a passing functional trace says nothing about whether a timing exception is valid (@sec-feedback-verification-trust), students must also explain what each check can and cannot see, using cases drawn from instructor-curated defects or shared repositories of failed runs.

[^fn-cdc-metastability-c12]: **Clock-domain crossing metastability**: When an asynchronous signal transitions within the setup and hold aperture of a receiving flip-flop, the register output can hover at an indeterminate intermediate voltage for an unpredictable duration [@Cummings2008CDC]. Zero-delay RTL simulation does not model setup and hold timing, so a crossing that could go metastable in silicon resolves to a clean binary value ($0$ or $1$), hiding synchronization failures that can appear as intermittent faults in fabricated silicon.

[^fn-sdc-false-path-c12]: **Static timing false-path declarations**: A timing constraint declared via `set_false_path` in an SDC file instructs static timing analysis tools to ignore signal propagation delays along specified paths. Declaring a false path on a path that is physically and logically exercisable silences real timing violations, so synthesis and layout tools stop optimizing that path, and the resulting silicon can fail at operating speed.

Students also need practice constructing better designs and better experiments. In a complementary exercise, a student first predicts a bottleneck and proposes a change, then gives an agent a bounded opportunity to investigate the same problem. The student compares the prediction, the agent's proposal, and the measured outcome before changing one part of the automated process, such as the performance counters exposed to the agent. Comparisons across repeated runs and workloads withheld from development can then test whether the revised process finds useful designs more consistently or at lower total cost. Assessment should examine the student's causal explanation, experimental choices, and ability to apply them to an unfamiliar workload alongside the quality of the resulting design.

Where commercial EDA licenses are available, students can extend these exercises by comparing OpenROAD and Yosys reports against industrial signoff reports to see which measurements and modeling assumptions carry across toolchains. A semester-long course can follow the sequence of this book, moving from the architectural question and the physical pressures behind it through the design life cycle, representations, methods, environments, and verification feedback, and concluding with cross-stack coordination, evaluation rigor, human ownership, and community infrastructure. The design principles developed across the chapters then serve as a practical exit test: students should be able to formulate and investigate an unfamiliar architectural problem, diagnose the returned evidence, and explain which parts of the work benefit from learned models.

While instructors can adopt these laboratory exercises locally inside their own courses, published research raises a broader coordination question: how can readers tell which parts of an automated design study received independent audit? Artifact evaluation committees at venues such as the International Symposium on Computer Architecture, the International Symposium on Microarchitecture, and the conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems, or comparable review tracks at the Design Automation Conference, could pilot an Autonomous Workflow Certified (AWC) badge grounded in computational reproducibility standards [@Stodden2010ReproducibleResearch; @StoddenEtAl2016Science].[^fn-awc-badge-c12] Just as ACM artifact badges distinguish whether an artifact is publicly available, verified as functional and reusable, or independently reproduced [@ACM2020ArtifactBadging], an AWC badge could record which of the workflow checks developed in this book were independently verified: replay under pinned environments, cryptographic lineage, total workflow-cost accounting, surrogate calibration against signoff tools, or physical closure on an open manufacturable PDK.

To prevent overclaiming, the badge would have to state the exact scope reviewers checked, whether computational repeatability for a simulator study, surrogate calibration against a reference flow, or physical closure in a named open PDK, without implying that every badged paper passed all three. Even full physical closure in an open flow does not establish commercial foundry signoff, electrostatic-discharge protection, process, voltage, and temperature yield qualification, or package thermo-mechanical reliability, and artifact review neither replaces measurements on fabricated silicon nor authorizes commercial tapeout. Stating the audited scope explicitly lets readers treat the badge as verifiable evidence of specific workflow checks rather than a blanket guarantee of hardware readiness.

[^fn-awc-badge-c12]: **Autonomous Workflow Certified badge**: AWC is a proposed designation in this chapter that extends computational reproducibility principles to an explicitly scoped review of an automated design workflow. The cited work motivates reproducibility practice; it does not establish this badge [@Stodden2010ReproducibleResearch; @StoddenEtAl2016Science].

## Open Questions {#sec-ecosystem-open-questions}

The questions that close each chapter mark where established engineering practice gives way to open research. At the community level, those unsolved problems sit where cross-team comparability, physical silicon measurements, and intellectual-property protection pull against one another:

- **When a design wins on an open predictive PDK, when does it still win under commercial foundry signoff?** Academic studies rely on open kits such as ASAP7 or mature nodes such as SKY130 to evaluate generated microarchitectures, yet sub-5\ nm commercial processes introduce multi-patterning rules, high via resistance, and nonlinear cell-delay effects that simpler decks omit. Much as wind-tunnel scale models predict full-scale flight only while key similarity numbers hold and fail once boundary-layer transitions flip drag rankings, we need systematic correlation studies and few-shot calibration methods that show which microarchitectural trade-offs hold across process nodes and which flip when evaluated on commercial extraction decks.

- **How can a benchmark consortium audit closed-loop design claims when foundry decks and proprietary models cannot be shared?** To verify a Layer 3 benchmark submission, independent reviewers must confirm that the team kept the evaluation constraints locked, ran a matched baseline, and reported its full workflow cost ($C_{\text{workflow}} = \langle C_{\text{compute}}, C_{\text{license}}, C_{\text{human}} \rangle$), even when foundry NDAs forbid releasing the process deck or transistor netlist. We still need practical attestation protocols and enclave-isolated evaluation harnesses that let outside auditors verify which tools ran, which constraints were enforced, and how much compute and license time was spent without exposing confidential silicon libraries.

- **How can teams share failed physical-design runs without leaking confidential product details or stripping away the signals that surrogates need?** Sharing unroutable floorplans, negative timing slack distributions, and power-grid violations helps cure survivorship bias in training datasets, but a series of abandoned layouts can also reveal a company's die dimensions, macro floorplan, and clock-frequency targets. We need graph-anonymization methods and formal privacy guarantees that strip out recognizable product geometry while preserving the local congestion and timing patterns that show a surrogate where physical implementation breaks down.

- **How can we instrument low-cost silicon shuttles at mature nodes so their measurements help calibrate surrogates for modern design search?** MPW runs at 130\ nm and 180\ nm bring the cost of fabricated silicon down to a few hundred dollars, but their planar transistors and tens-of-megahertz clock trees cannot directly validate a 3\ W, 3\ nm-class mobile compute subsystem. What the community lacks are standardized on-die test harnesses that combine ring-oscillator arrays, transient voltage-droop monitors, and programmable traffic generators on cheap shuttle tiles to measure systematically where pre-silicon timing and power models drift from real silicon.

- **How can benchmark suites refresh their tasks to prevent model memorization without breaking comparisons across years and tool versions?** The benchmark-renewal practices in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect aim to keep evaluation tasks ahead of pretraining contamination even as underlying simulators, synthesis tools, and container environments change. Fixed register-transfer benchmarks quickly leak into model training sets, yet ad hoc benchmark updates make it impossible to compare new results against earlier papers. The field still needs parameterized benchmark generators that can produce fresh, non-isomorphic design tasks of known difficulty while automatically recalibrating reference baselines whenever the toolchain changes.

## Summary and Immediate Action Items {#sec-ecosystem-coda}

The MPC79 fabrication story that opened this chapter succeeded because it joined two kinds of work: design rules that individual engineers could apply at their own desks and shared brokering services that let them test what they built in silicon. An AI-native architecture ecosystem needs the same division of labor. A structured record schema pays off when another laboratory's tools can parse it without guesswork, and a shared reference flow pays off when researchers can run the physical checks their claims require. Individual teams can adopt the local engineering practices right away while consortium standards and shared infrastructure take shape, though whether those community investments make cross-organization claims genuinely comparable remains an empirical question the field must test.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Separate local discipline from shared dependencies.** A team can adopt provenance, failure retention, matched baselines, and total-cost accounting now; cross-team comparison, silicon claims, and public rankings additionally depend on shared schemas, fabrication paths, and neutral governance.
- **Prepare records for another reader.** Retain units, versions, status meanings, costs, and dependencies so a collaborator can interpret a run without relying on its author's memory.
- **Keep failures with their context.** Preserve inputs and diagnostic returns, distinguish tool failures from rejected designs, and review disclosure risks before contributing records to a shared repository.
- **Name the implementation path.** Identify which modeled checks a team's open flow supports and what additional process access or fabricated measurements a broader claim would require.
- **Make a comparison reusable.** Version the task, comparator, checks, and workflow costs together so another group can attempt the same comparison and report where it differs.
- **Teach diagnosis through retained artifacts.** Use shadow audits and fault-injection exercises to let students explain failures, select checks, and recognize what those checks cannot observe.
:::

The questions posed across this book are starting points rather than a finished research agenda, and they leave ample room for students and practitioners to contribute before these community norms are settled. When a new study shows that two tools interpret an environmental contract differently, that a shared benchmark omits a critical physical constraint, or that an anonymized failure trace still reveals too much about a commercial chip, progress will depend on the same engineering habits developed throughout these chapters: state an explicit question, name the check that can answer it, and record what the experiment leaves unresolved. Carried forward to the next workload, model family, or fabrication node, that discipline keeps computer architecture grounded in evidence even as its tools and methods change.
